title: Dephasing-powered open quantum-dot battery
authors: Alok Nath Singh, Rafael Sánchez, Andrew N. Jordan
abstract: We propose a simple realization of an open quantum battery powered by local dephasing. The setup consists of a triple-quantum-dot chain coupled at one end to a thermal reservoir, with the dot at the opposite end strongly detuned to form a high-energy storage element. Local dephasing populates this highly excited state and autonomously drives the system into a nonequilibrium steady state with high ergotropic efficiency. We find a limit where the ergotropic efficiency approaches unity, while the ergotropy itself approaches one-third of the energy detuning. We characterize the battery through its energy-storage performance, charging time, and stability, showing that the charged state remains long-lived after the dephasing source is switched off. We then demonstrate two complementary protocols for extracting the stored energy. First, nearly all the available ergotropy can be recovered through a simple cyclic unitary protocol involving only modulation of the detuned-dot gate. Second, coupling the detuned dot to an electronic load allows the extraction of electrochemical work exceeding the initial ergotropy, thereby accessing part of the battery's passive energy. Our results establish local dephasing as an autonomous resource for charging open quantum batteries and demonstrate simple routes for extracting the resulting stored energy in experimentally accessible mesoscopic platforms.
summary: This paper demonstrates that local dephasing can autonomously charge an open quantum dot battery by populating a high-energy, weakly coupled state. The stored energy, quantified by ergotropy, can then be efficiently extracted through either coherent unitary protocols or by coupling the system to an external electronic load. This establishes dephasing as a viable, controllable resource for quantum energy storage.
main_problem: The paper proposes and analyzes a mechanism for creating and extracting energy from an open quantum battery powered autonomously by local dephasing.
main_result: Local dephasing acts as an autonomous resource to charge the battery into a non-equilibrium steady state, and the stored energy can be recovered via unitary modulation or by coupling to an external load.
method: The dynamics are modeled using an open quantum system approach, solved via a Lindblad master equation in the eigenbasis of the quantum dot chain.
model_or_system: The system is a triple-quantum-dot (TQD) chain coupled to a thermal reservoir and subjected to local dephasing ($\gamma$). The model operates in the strong-Coulomb blockade and high-detuning limits.
key_observables: Ergotropic efficiency, stored energy (ergotropy), charging time, and the steady-state populations of the quantum dots.
important_parameters: Local dephasing rate ($\gamma$), detuning ($\Delta$), hopping ($\Omega$), and reservoir temperature ($T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the high-detuning limit ($\Delta \gg \Omega$) and assumes the dephasing source is the charging resource.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the TQD setup, energy level schematics, charging dynamics showing population transfer, and the evolution of stored work ($W$) relative to passive energy ($E_{passive}$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model (TQD, reservoir, dephasing). It then analyzes the steady-state charging process, demonstrating energy storage. Finally, it details two distinct protocols for energy extraction: a unitary cycle and coupling to an electronic load.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and energy harvesting in mesoscopic quantum systems, providing a concrete physical realization of quantum batteries driven by environmental noise (dephasing).

figures.caption: Figure 1. Dephasing-powered open quantum battery consist- ing of a triple-quantum-dot chain. (a) The rightmost dot is coupled to an electron reservoir at temperature T and chemi- cal potential µ with a tunneling strength Γ. The leftmost dot is detuned by ∆, while the other two have a common energy ε. A nearby dephasing source is coupled to it with strength γ and serves as the sole charging resource. (b) Schematic representation of the quantum dot levels (solid lines) and the hybridized eigenenergies Eg, Ee, and Ed (dashed lines).

Figure 2. Charging dynamics of the dephasing-powered quantum battery for ∆= 100Ω, Γ = 0.1Ω, kBT = Ω, µ = ε, and γ = 10Ω. (a) Populations of the empty state and the three single-electron energy eigenstates. (b) Internal energy E = Tr( ˆH0ˆρ), passive-state energy Epassive, and ergotropy W. Dephasing drives the system into a highly excited nonequilib- rium steady state while maintaining a large extractable-work component. (c) Ergotropic efficiency W/E, which approaches ≈73% in the steady state.

Figure 3. Steady-state battery performance as a function of barrier detuning ∆, for different cases of dephasing strength γ. The remaining parameters are fixed at Γ = 0.1Ω, kBT = Ω, and µ = ε, with dephasing acting on the barrier dot. Panel (a): steady-state internal energy Ess/Ω. The stored energy increases mainly with ∆, reflecting the increasing energy of the populated barrier-like state, while its dependence on γ is much weaker. Panel (b): ergotropic efficiency Wss/Ess. The efficiency remains high over a broad parameter range, indicating that the dephasing-induced active state is robust against changes in ∆and γ.

Figure 4. Ergotropic charging time as a function of dephasing strength for several barrier detunings. Increasing the dephas- ing strength substantially reduces the charging time, showing that γ provides a kinetic control knob for the battery. Larger detuning slows the charging process because the high-energy barrier state is more weakly hybridized with the low-energy states. Parameters: Γ = 0.1Ω, kBT = Ω, and µ = ε.

Figure 5. Stability of the charged quantum battery after the dephasing source is switched off. (a) Internal energy E, passive energy Epassive, and ergotropy W in the absence of phonon relaxation, demonstrating strongly suppressed relax- ation through the thermal reservoir. (b) Ergotropy retention in the presence of phonon-induced relaxation for different val- ues of κph. In each case, phonon relaxation is included during both charging and storage, and the battery is initially charged to 95% of its corresponding steady-state ergotropy. Other pa- rameters are the same as in Fig. 2.
